title: Insomnia — Poor Sleep (Anidra): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Sleep Routine
excerpt: Tossing and turning all night, waking up again and again, opening your eyes too early in the morning and feeling tired all day — insomnia is a very common problem today. Learn the causes from the Ayurvedic view, how much sleep is needed, what to eat and what to avoid, the right sleep routine, yoga, safe home remedies, and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“As soon as I lie down, thoughts start racing in my mind and I can't sleep for hours” — this complaint is heard today from people of every age. Mobile phones, working late at night, stress and changing routines have affected sleep the most. Without good sleep come irritability, poor concentration, headache and digestive problems, and over time the risk of high BP, diabetes and weight gain also rises.

The good news is that in most people sleep improves a great deal with the right daily routine, diet, ways to calm the mind and good sleep habits. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What is insomnia?

Most adults need about 7 hours or more of sleep every day. Insomnia does not mean only sleeping fewer hours; it also means poor quality of sleep. Its main forms are:

  • Not falling asleep for a long time after lying down
  • Waking up again and again at night and being unable to fall asleep again
  • Waking up very early in the morning
  • Not feeling fresh in the morning even after sleeping all night, with tiredness and sluggishness all day

Insomnia for a few days is often due to some stress, travel or illness and settles on its own. But if it continues three or more nights a week, for more than three months, it is considered chronic insomnia and needs proper treatment.

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda, sleep is counted among the three upastambhas (sub-pillars) of life, along with food and brahmacharya. Acharya Charaka has described the importance of sleep as follows:

निद्रायत्तं सुखं दुःखं पुष्टिः कार्श्यं बलाबलम् ।
वृषता क्लीबता ज्ञानमज्ञानं जीवितं न च ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana 21

Meaning: Happiness and sorrow, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness, virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, and life and death — all these depend on sleep. In other words, proper sleep is the foundation of health.

According to Ayurveda, the main cause of insomnia is increased Vata (worry, overthinking, dry-cold food, irregular routine) and often increased Pitta (anger, pressure of too much work, staying up late). When the mind (manas) is tired and the senses withdraw from their objects, natural sleep comes; aggravated Vata does not let the mind settle. So the basis of care is — calming Vata-Pitta, steadying the mind and a regular routine.

Main causes

  • Stress, anxiety, sadness (depression) and constantly running thoughts
  • Changing sleep and wake times daily, shift work, long naps in the day
  • Using the mobile, TV or laptop for long before sleeping
  • Tea-coffee, cold drinks, smoking or alcohol in the evening
  • A heavy or very late dinner, acidity and bloating
  • Pain (back, knees), frequent urination, cough or breathing trouble
  • Snoring and pauses in breathing during sleep (sleep apnoea), restlessness in the legs (restless legs)
  • Overactive thyroid, menopause; some medicines (such as steroids, some BP and asthma medicines)

Tests

Insomnia can be a disease in itself and also a symptom of another problem. The doctor or Vaidya asks about your routine, stress, medicines and illnesses. Keeping a sleep diary for a few weeks — when you went to bed, when sleep came, how many times you woke, how you felt in the day — helps a lot in understanding the cause. If needed, blood tests such as thyroid and iron (anaemia), and a sleep study if there is loud snoring or pauses in breathing, may be done.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

According to Ayurveda, dinner should be light, warm and early, so that the stomach is not heavy at bedtime and Vata stays calm.

What to eat

  • Dinner 2–3 hours before sleeping — light food like moong dal, khichdi, dalia, vegetables and roti
  • Lukewarm milk before sleeping (if milk suits you)
  • A little desi ghee in food — according to Ayurveda it calms Vata (in heart disease or high cholesterol ask your doctor)
  • Seasonal fruits like banana, apple, papaya; soaked almonds and walnuts
  • Enough water during the day (do not drink too much water at night, so you don't have to get up again and again)

What to avoid

  • Tea, coffee, cold drinks and energy drinks after midday
  • Alcohol and smoking — alcohol may bring sleep quickly, but sleep breaks again and again at night
  • Very spicy, oily-fried, heavy food at night and late-night snacks
  • Very sweet food or chocolate just before sleeping

The right sleep routine

In Ayurveda, Dinacharya and Ratricharya (day and night routine) are considered the biggest medicine for sleep. Adopt these habits (today called “sleep hygiene”):

  • Sleep and wake at the same time every day — even on holidays; try to sleep by 10–11 PM
  • Switch off the mobile, TV and laptop at least 1 hour before sleeping
  • The bedroom should be dark, quiet, airy and neither too hot nor too cold; use the bed only for sleeping
  • If sleep does not come in 20–30 minutes, get up, do something calm in another room in dim light and return only when sleepy
  • Do not take long naps in the day; get morning sunlight and exercise daily (but no heavy exercise just before bed)
  • Before sleeping, wash hands and feet with lukewarm water and do Padabhyanga (gentle massage of the soles with lukewarm sesame oil)

Yoga and pranayama

In the evening, Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari pranayama, meditation and Shavasana (Yoga Nidra) are considered helpful in calming the mind; Balasana and Viparita Karani can also be done. Caution: in glaucoma, high blood pressure, neck problems or pregnancy, do not do inverted poses without asking your doctor. Learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe home remedies

  • Padabhyanga: gentle massage of the soles with lukewarm sesame or coconut oil before sleeping
  • Shiro-abhyanga: gentle massage of the head with lukewarm oil a few times a week
  • Lukewarm milk: before sleeping (if milk suits you, and in diabetes if the doctor permits)
  • Deep breathing: lying down and slowly taking long breaths in and out, or recalling the good things of the day in your mind

These remedies are only supportive. If there is no improvement in two to three weeks, see a Vaidya or doctor.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for insomnia, such as — Ashwagandha, Brahmi, Jatamansi, Shankhpushpi and Tagar. Procedures like Shirodhara (a stream of medicated oil or liquid on the forehead) and Nasya under a Vaidya's supervision are also mentioned. However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age, the cause of insomnia and current medicines.
  • Do not suddenly stop your current medicines for sleep, depression or anxiety on your own — stopping some sleeping pills suddenly can cause restlessness, anxiety and even worse sleep; reducing them is done only slowly under a doctor's supervision.
  • Some herbs can change the effect of sleeping pills, BP, diabetes or thyroid medicines; Ashwagandha can change thyroid levels — so tell your doctor everything.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any medicine or sleeping pill only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of over-the-counter sleeping pills and claims like “guaranteed deep sleep in one dose”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Sleeplessness with deep sadness, hopelessness, or thoughts of harming yourself — contact a doctor or helpline immediately
  • Loud snoring, pauses in breathing during sleep or waking up choking, and great sleepiness in the day
  • So much sleepiness or drowsiness in the day that you doze off while driving or working
  • Chest pain, breathlessness, a fast heartbeat or heavy sweating at night
  • Hardly sleeping for several days and yet having too much energy, restlessness or unusual behaviour
  • Sudden worsening of sleep with confusion in the elderly; or insomnia lasting more than three months

Summary — points to remember

  • About 7 hours or more of sleep daily; keep sleep and wake times the same
  • Screens off before sleeping; a dark and quiet room
  • Light and early dinner; no tea-coffee after evening
  • Padabhyanga, pranayama, meditation; exercise and sunlight in the day
  • Do not start sleeping pills on your own or stop them suddenly; medicines only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya
